title: 011 — Databricks AI Runtime (GA) and Agent Memory (Beta)
html:
011 — Databricks AI Runtime (GA) and Agent Memory (Beta)

The one idea: Databricks shipped two pieces for teams building AI on their own data. AI Runtime (generally available) is serverless GPU compute for training and fine-tuning models where the data already lives, with no separate GPU cluster to run. Agent Memory (Beta) gives agents managed conversation history and long-term memory, stored in Lakebase Postgres in your own workspace.

Added 2026-10-26 · Announced 2026-10-20 and 2026-10-21 by Databricks

1. What it is

AI Runtime (AIR) Agent Memory
Status Generally available Beta
What Managed, serverless GPU training environment, including multinode runs on RDMA-connected clusters (A100 and H100 named in examples) Managed sessions (ordered messages, tool calls and results) and managed memory (user profile, preferences, domain facts, workflows)
Where Databricks serverless GPU pools Lakebase (serverless Postgres) in your workspace
How you use it CLI, notebooks or IDE; production runs via a few lines of YAML in a Lakeflow pipeline Agent Bricks CLI; plugins that log and load context automatically, plus tools the agent can call
Governance Unity Catalog for data, checkpoints and logs; VM isolation, PrivateLink, egress controls Read, export and delete memory per user; retention instructions; models reached through Unity Gateway

2. Why it matters

  • Fine-tuning without a platform team. Training a model on company data used to mean running Kubernetes or SLURM GPU clusters and copying data out. AIR keeps the data under Unity Catalog and handles GPU provisioning and health checks for you.
  • Agents that remember. Most agent prototypes forget everything between sessions. Agent Memory stores history and distilled facts, merges duplicates, and overwrites facts that newer conversations contradict.
  • One governance model. Training data, checkpoints and agent memories all sit in governed workspace storage. That makes data-protection deletion requests and audits easier.

3. How it works

---
title: Agent Memory — sessions in, distilled memory out
---
flowchart LR
    S["Agent session<br/>(messages, tool calls)"] -->|"logged automatically"| L[("Lakebase<br/>sessions")]
    L --> P["Background pipeline:<br/>extract, de-duplicate,<br/>resolve contradictions"]
    P --> M[("Lakebase<br/>memory")]
    M -->|"index loaded at session start<br/>+ hybrid search on demand"| S

Each session is recorded as is. A background pipeline, run on a schedule or on demand, turns sessions into durable memory entries. At the start of a new session, the agent loads an index of what it knows. During the session it searches memory with combined keyword and semantic search.

AIR works like other serverless compute. A command lands on a warm GPU pool in seconds. Data streams through the provided loaders, such as UCVolumeDataset. MLflow records the run, and --watch streams the logs.

4. How to use it

AI Runtime:

  1. Start with the AIR quickstart docs or the ai-runtime-cookbook repository.
  2. Run a first job from the CLI, and add --watch to follow the logs.
  3. To move it to production, add the job to a Lakeflow pipeline in YAML, which gives you scheduling, priority and pre-emption.
  4. Track spend in the Databricks billing system tables.

Agent Memory:

  1. Follow the quickstart to provision memory in a Lakebase project.
  2. Add the memory plugin to an existing agent, using the "add memory to an existing agent" tutorial.
  3. Set retention instructions and test per-user deletion before real users arrive.

In practice: try prompting and RAG first. Fine-tune with AIR only when the model needs to learn a format or behaviour it can't get from retrieval.

5. Trade-offs and limits

  • Vendor claims. The speed-ups (AIR) and the roughly 3x higher pass rate with 31% fewer tokens (Agent Memory) come from Databricks and its customers, not independent tests.
  • Pricing and quotas aren't stated in either post. Check the pricing pages and your region's GPU availability before you plan.
  • Agent Memory is Beta. The APIs may change. Stored memory is personal data, so plan for retention, consent and deletion from the start.
  • Fine-tuning is rarely step one. It adds evaluation, versioning and serving work on top of training.
  • Adopt now or wait? AIR is ready for teams already on Databricks that need GPUs. Prototype with Agent Memory, but wait for GA before production use.

6. Where it fits

  • LLM engineering and RAG: when retrieval is enough and when fine-tuning helps.
  • AI/ML foundations: training, fine-tuning and evaluation basics.
  • Databricks platform: Unity Catalog, serverless compute and Lakeflow.
  • Databricks transactions GA: the other big Databricks release this month.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. When would you fine-tune a model on AIR instead of improving retrieval?
  2. What's the difference between an agent's session history and its memory, and why store both?
  3. How should a memory pipeline handle a user who changes a preference?
  4. What data-protection duties come with storing agent memory per user?
  5. Which numbers would you measure yourself before trusting the vendor's speed-up claims?

Sources

  • Introducing Agent Memory on Databricks — Databricks blog, 20 Oct 2026
